For all $1\le i,j\le n$ one has $X_iX_j=X_jX_i$ in $\mathbb Z[S_n]$, hence in
$R[S_n]$ for every commutative ring $R$; that is, the Jucys-Murphy elements
commute pairwise, and the subalgebra they generate is commutative.

Let $n\ge1$ and let $R$ be a commutative ring. In the group ring $R[S_n]$ of
the symmetric group on $\{1,\dots,n\}$
([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]],
[[def-symmetric-group]], [[def-group-ring]]), where $(j\ k)$ denotes the
transposition of the distinct entries $j,k\in\{1,\dots,n\}$
([[def-symmetric-group]]), the **Jucys-Murphy elements** are
$$X_1:=0,\qquad X_k:=\sum_{j=1}^{k-1}(j\ k)\in R[S_n]\qquad(2\le k\le n).$$
Each $X_k$ is a finite sum of group elements with coefficient $1$, so the
formula already defines an element of the integral group ring
$\mathbb Z[S_n]$, and its image under the base change
$\mathbb Z[S_n]\to R[S_n]$ is the displayed element
([[def-restriction-and-extension-of-scalars]]); for $1\le k\le m\le n$ the element
$X_k$ of $R[S_m]$, computed in the subgroup
$S_m=\operatorname{Sym}(\{1,\dots,m\})\subseteq S_n$ of permutations fixing
$m+1,\dots,n$, maps to $X_k$ under the inclusion $S_m\hookrightarrow S_n$.
Equivalently $X_k=T_k-T_{k-1}$, where $T_k=\sum_{1\le i<j\le k}(i\ j)$ is the
sum of all transpositions in $S_k$.

Let $n\ge1$. (a) The elements $X_1,\dots,X_n$ act diagonally in the Young
basis of the previous item: for every standard tableau $T$ of size $n$ and
every $k$, $X_kv_T=c_T(k)v_T$, and the joint eigenspaces are
one-dimensional, indexed by the standard tableaux. (b) A vector
$\alpha=(a_1,\dots,a_n)\in\mathbb Z^n$ occurs as the joint eigenvalue vector
of a $v_T$, equivalently $\alpha=\operatorname{Cont}(T)$ for a standard
tableau $T$, if and only if: (1) $a_1=0$; (2) for every $q>1$ at least one of
$a_q-1,a_q+1$ occurs among $a_1,\dots,a_{q-1}$; (3) if $a_p=a_q$ with $p<q$,
then both $a_p-1$ and $a_p+1$ occur among $a_{p+1},\dots,a_{q-1}$. The
association $T\mapsto\operatorname{Cont}(T)$ is a bijection from the standard
tableaux of size $n$ onto this set.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring and let $I_1,\ldots,I_r$ be pairwise comaximal ideals, where $r\ge1$. Then the canonical map
$$ R\longrightarrow \prod_{i=1}^r R/I_i,\qquad x\longmapsto(x+I_1,\ldots,x+I_r) $$
is surjective, its kernel is $\bigcap_{i=1}^r I_i$, and
$$ \bigcap_{i=1}^r I_i=\prod_{i=1}^r I_i. $$
Equivalently,
$$ R/\prod_{i=1}^r I_i\cong\prod_{i=1}^r R/I_i. $$

For $H\le G$, restriction forgets from $\mathbb Z[G]$ to $\mathbb Z[H]$. For a left $H$-module $M$, set $\operatorname{Ind}_H^G M=\mathbb Z[G]\otimes_{\mathbb Z[H]}M$ and $\operatorname{Coind}_H^G M=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb Z[H]}(\mathbb Z[G],M)$, with $G$ acting on the latter by $(g\varphi)(x)=\varphi(xg)$.
If $H\le G$ and a left (respectively right) coset transversal is supplied, then $\mathbb Z[G]$ is free as a right (respectively left) $\mathbb Z[H]$-module on it.

Fix a splitting $p$-modular system $(K,\mathcal O,k)$ for a finite group $G$.
A **$p$-block idempotent** is a primitive central idempotent of $\mathcal O G$
or, after reduction, of $kG$.

If $e$ is such an idempotent, the corresponding **block** is the two-sided
ideal

$$B=\mathcal OGe\qquad\text{or}\qquad B=kGe.$$

The primitive central idempotents are pairwise orthogonal and sum to $1$, so
the algebra splits as a direct product of its block summands.

For every commutative unital ring $R$ and $n\ge0$, every element of $Z(RS_n)$ is an $R$-linear combination of evaluations of integral monomial symmetric polynomials at $L_r=\sum_{a<r}(a,r)$. Conversely every symmetric polynomial evaluation is central. In particular $Z(RS_n)=R[L_1,\ldots,L_n]^{\mathrm{sym}}$, where the right side denotes evaluations of symmetric polynomials, not invariants of an action on the group algebra. No integer is inverted.

Let $n\ge0$, let $\lambda\vdash n$, and let $\Omega_\lambda$ be the finite set
of $\lambda$-tabloids; for a $\lambda$-tableau $t$ write $\{t\}$ for its
tabloid ([[def-young-subgroup-tabloid-and-permutation-module]]). The
**integral tabloid module** is the free abelian group on $\Omega_\lambda$,

$$M^\lambda_{\mathbb Z}:=\mathbb Z^{(\Omega_\lambda)} =\Bigl\{\sum_{T\in\Omega_\lambda}a_T\,T:\ a_T\in\mathbb Z,\ \text{only finitely many }a_T\ne0\Bigr\},$$

with the tabloids as standard $\mathbb Z$-basis
([[def-free-module-on-a-set-and-standard-basis]]). The left action of $S_n$ on
tabloids extends $\mathbb Z$-linearly to $M^\lambda_{\mathbb Z}$, so that
$M^\lambda_{\mathbb Z}$ is a $\mathbb Z[S_n]$-module. For every $\lambda$-tableau
$t$ put

$$\kappa_t:=\sum_{\gamma\in C_t}\operatorname{sgn}(\gamma)\gamma \in\mathbb Z[S_n],\qquad e_t:=\kappa_t\cdot\{t\}=\sum_{\gamma\in C_t}\operatorname{sgn}(\gamma)\, \{\gamma\cdot t\}\in M^\lambda_{\mathbb Z},$$

the **integral column polytabloid**; every coefficient lies in
$\{0,1,-1\}$ ([[def-column-antisymmetrizer-polytabloid-and-specht-module]]).
The **integral Specht lattice** is the $\mathbb Z[S_n]$-submodule

$$S^\lambda_{\mathbb Z}:=\text{the }\mathbb Z\text{-span of } \{\,e_s:\ s\text{ a }\lambda\text{-tableau}\,\}\subseteq M^\lambda_{\mathbb Z}.$$

For a commutative ring $R$ let $M^\lambda_R:=R^{(\Omega_\lambda)}$ be the free
$R$-module on the tabloids and let $S^\lambda_R\subseteq M^\lambda_R$ be the
$R$-span of the polytabloids $\sum_{\gamma\in C_t}\operatorname{sgn}(\gamma)
\{\gamma\cdot t\}$, $t$ a $\lambda$-tableau. The **standard polytabloids** are
the $e_s$ with $s$ a standard $\lambda$-tableau
([[def-young-tableau-standard-tableau-and-shape]]).

This item records three facts. First, the standard polytabloids form a
$\mathbb Z$-basis of $S^\lambda_{\mathbb Z}$, so the integral Specht lattice has
explicit finite rank. Second, for every commutative ring $R$ the canonical map
$R\otimes_{\mathbb Z}S^\lambda_{\mathbb Z}\to R\otimes_{\mathbb Z}
M^\lambda_{\mathbb Z}\cong M^\lambda_R$ is injective onto $S^\lambda_R$: the
lattice is a direct summand of the free tabloid module and is compatible with
base change, including rings of prime characteristic. Third, for
$\lambda=\varnothing$ the module has rank one and is generated by the empty
polytabloid.

Let $G$ be a finite group and let $k$ be an algebraically closed field with
$\operatorname{char} k \nmid |G|$. Then there are positive integers
$n_1,\ldots,n_r$ such that

$$ k[G]\cong\prod_{i=1}^r M_{n_i}(k) $$

as $k$-algebras.

boundaries.evidence: Statement and proof steps: Rank-zero empty tuple gives the single block k. Positive rank construction and restriction remain separate from S_-1, which is never used.

Zero is an allowed residue and content entry: step 1.1 factors the minimal polynomial over all a in F_p including a = 0, step 2.1 keeps the exponent m_0, and step 5.1 sums over every i in Z/p including i = 0.
For n = 1 the decomposition of step 5.1 collapses to the single-node projectors P_{1,a} and E_iM = e((i))M, and the identities of steps 2.1 and 3.1 apply verbatim.
Statement and proof steps: Integer triangular center spanning and scalar-plus-nilpotent local centers apply over every characteristic, including p=2, without denominator or splitting.
The extreme residues 0 and p − 1 are ordinary members of Z/p: the direct sum of step 5.1 runs over the whole group and step 7.1 treats every i uniformly.
Only finite index sets and finite orbit sums are selected: the construction of step 5.1 uses the finite set F_p of residues and finite orbits, and no choice principle is used.

derivations.claim: *Eigenvalues in $\mathbb F_p$.* Let $h_r\in\mathbb Q[X]$ be the minimal polynomial of $L_r$ acting on the left regular module $\mathbb QS_n$. Over $\mathbb C$ the regular module is the direct sum of the complex Specht modules with multiplicities, and by [F2] the eigenvalues of $L_r$ on that module are the integers $c_T(r)$, the contents of the node containing $r$, over all standard tableaux $T$ of $n$ nodes; hence $h_r=\prod_{a\in E_r}(X-a)$ is squarefree with the integer roots in the finite set $E_r$. The group-basis coordinates of $h_r(L_r)$ are integers and vanish over $\mathbb Q$, so this identity holds already in $\mathbb ZS_n$. Reduction of coefficients modulo $p$ therefore gives $h_r(L_r)=0$ in $kS_n$, so the minimal polynomial $f_r$ of $L_r$ on the regular module $kS_n$ divides the reduction $\bar h_r=\prod_{a\in E_r}(X-\bar a)$ in $k[X]$, and every root of $f_r$ lies in the image $\mathbb F_p$ of $\mathbb Z$ in $k$.

*Antipode invariance.* The antipode $\sigma:kS_n\to kS_n$, $\sigma(g)=g^{-1}$, is an anti-automorphism fixing every transposition, hence fixes each $L_r$ and therefore each $P_{r,a}\in k[L_r]$ and each $e(\mathbf i)$.

*An integral central identity.* In $\mathbb ZS_n$ one has $\prod_{r=1}^n(u+L_r)=\sum_{g\in S_n}u^{c(g)}g$, where $c(g)$ is the number of cycles, including fixed points. To prove this by induction, regard $S_{n-1}$ as fixing $n$. A term multiplied by $u$ leaves $n$ fixed and adds one cycle. A term multiplied by $(a,n)$ inserts $n$ in the cycle containing $a$, without changing its cycle count. Conversely, deleting a nonfixed $n$ from its cycle uniquely recovers the permutation in $S_{n-1}$ and the transposition used. Thus every permutation occurs exactly once. Comparing coefficients, each elementary symmetric polynomial $C_s$ in $L_1,\ldots,L_n$ is a sum of all permutations with $n-s$ cycles and hence is central; the identity and centrality remain true after reduction to $k$.

*Primary projectors.* Write $f_r=\prod_{a\in\mathbb F_p}(X-a)^{m_a}$ with $m_a\ge0$. For $a\ne b$ the ideals $\big((X-a)^{m_a}\big)$ and $\big((X-b)^{m_b}\big)$ of $k[X]$ are comaximal, since two powers of distinct linear polynomials are coprime and Bezout gives $1=u(X)(X-a)^{m_a}+v(X)(X-b)^{m_b}$. By [F4] applied to the ring $k[X]/(f_r)$ and its comaximal ideals, the canonical map $k[X]/(f_r)\to\prod_{a:m_a>0}k[X]/\big((X-a)^{m_a}\big)$ is an isomorphism; let $\varepsilon_{r,a}$ be the preimage of the idempotent supported at the $a$-th factor when $m_a>0$, and put $\varepsilon_{r,a}=0$ when $m_a=0$. Then $\sum_a\varepsilon_{r,a}=1$, $\varepsilon_{r,a}^2=\varepsilon_{r,a}$, $\varepsilon_{r,a}\varepsilon_{r,b}=0$ for $a\ne b$, and $(X-a)^{m_a}\varepsilon_{r,a}=0$ in $k[X]/(f_r)$. Substituting the algebra element $L_r$ for $X$ (legitimate because $f_r(L_r)=0$) gives elements $P_{r,a}:=\varepsilon_{r,a}(L_r)\in k[L_r]$ with $\sum_aP_{r,a}=1$, $P_{r,a}P_{r,b}=\delta_{a,b}P_{r,a}$ and $(L_r-a)^{m_a}P_{r,a}=0$.

*These are the primary projections.* Let $M$ be a finite-dimensional $kS_n$-module. Since the $P_{r,a}$ are polynomials in $L_r$, they commute with $L_r$ and with one another; as $1=\sum_aP_{r,a}$ one has $M=\sum_aP_{r,a}M$, and $(L_r-a)^{m_a}$ annihilates $P_{r,a}M$, so $P_{r,a}M\subseteq M_{r,a}$. Conversely, if $m\in M_{r,a}$, then $(L_r-a)^Nm=0$ for $N\ge m_a$, and for $b\ne a$ the element $L_r-b=(a-b)+(L_r-a)$ is invertible on the $a$-primary subspace because $(a-b)\in k^\times$ and $(L_r-a)$ is nilpotent there; from $P_{r,b}(L_r-b)^{m_b}=0$ we get $P_{r,b}m=0$ for $b\ne a$, whence $m=P_{r,a}m$. Thus $P_{r,a}M=M_{r,a}$ and $M=\bigoplus_aM_{r,a}$. The products $e(\mathbf i)=\prod_rP_{r,i_r}$ are idempotent, pairwise orthogonal and sum to $1$ by multiplicativity of the $P_{r,a}$; applying the same argument successively to the commuting operators $L_1,\dots,L_n$ gives $e(\mathbf i)M=M_{\mathbf i}$.

*Central CRT separates contents.* Choose $N\ge1$ such that $(L_r-i_r)^Ne(\mathbf i)=0$ for every $r$ and every tuple $\mathbf i$, using step 2.1 and the finiteness of the indices. On the commutative algebra summand $e(\mathbf i)k[L_1,\ldots,L_n]$ with identity $e(\mathbf i)$, the commuting elements $(L_r-i_r)e(\mathbf i)$ generate an ideal whose $D$-th power is zero for $D=n(N-1)+1$: every monomial of degree $D$ has a factor with exponent at least $N$. Thus $C_s-c_s(\mathbf i)$ belongs to that nilpotent ideal, where $c_s(\mathbf i)$ is the elementary symmetric function of the residues. The tuple $c(\mathbf i)=(c_1(\mathbf i),\ldots,c_n(\mathbf i))$ determines the content, because $\prod_r(X-i_r)=\sum_{s=0}^n(-1)^sc_s(\mathbf i)X^{n-s}$ determines the multiplicities of its distinct linear factors, over every characteristic. In $R=k[Y_1,\ldots,Y_n]$, the distinct content tuples therefore define distinct pairwise comaximal maximal ideals $\mathfrak m_\alpha=(Y_s-c_s(\alpha):1\le s\le n)$; their powers $\mathfrak m_\alpha^D$ are also pairwise comaximal, since expanding $1=(a+b)^{2D-1}$ for $a+b=1$ places every term in one of the two $D$-th powers. By [F4], choose $Q_\alpha\in R$ congruent to $1$ modulo $\mathfrak m_\alpha^D$ and to $0$ modulo every other $\mathfrak m_\beta^D$. The nilpotence just proved gives $Q_\alpha(C_1,\ldots,C_n)e(\mathbf i)=e(\mathbf i)$ when $\mathbf i\in I_\alpha$, and $0$ otherwise. Since the tuple idempotents sum to $1$, it follows that $Q_\alpha(C_1,\ldots,C_n)=\sum_{\mathbf i\in I_\alpha}e(\mathbf i)=e_\alpha$. This is central by step 1.3. Idempotency, pairwise orthogonality for distinct content classes, and $\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal C_n}e_\alpha=1$ follow from step 3.1 and the partition of all tuples into their content classes.

*The functor projectors.* Fix $i\in\mathbb F_p$ and $\alpha\in\mathcal C_{n-1}$. The primary projectors for $L_r$, $r<n$, computed in $kS_{n-1}$ agree with those in $kS_n$: the primary idempotents in $k[L_r]$ are uniquely determined by their congruences modulo the powers of the distinct linear factors of the minimal polynomial, and the inclusion preserves the polynomial relations of $L_r$. Summing once over each distinct sequence representing $\alpha$ gives $e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}=\sum_{\mathbf j\in I_\alpha}e((\mathbf j,i))=e_\alpha^{(n-1)}P_{n,i}$. By step 4.1 the first factor is central in $kS_{n-1}$, while the second commutes with $kS_{n-1}$ by [F1]; their product is therefore an idempotent commuting with that subgroup algebra. The sets $\{(\mathbf j,i):\mathbf j\in I_\alpha\}$ are disjoint for distinct pairs $(\alpha,i)$ and partition all tuples of length $n$. Consequently these idempotents are pairwise orthogonal and sum to $1$, and their images are $kS_{n-1}$-submodules. Grouping these actual direct summands by the last residue gives $\operatorname{Res}M=\bigoplus_{i\in\mathbb F_p}E_iM$. The indexing is by content classes throughout, so no content is counted twice.

*Every nonzero content summand has local center.* Fix $e=e_\alpha\ne0$. Since $e$ is central, $Z(e kS_n)=eZ(kS_n)$: an element central in the summand commutes with the complementary summand because their products vanish. By [F7] every element of this center is $ef(L)$ for a symmetric polynomial $f$ over $k$. For every $\mathbf i\in I_\alpha$, the difference $(f(L)-f(\mathbf i))e(\mathbf i)$ belongs to the nilpotent ideal of step 4.1; symmetry makes $f(\mathbf i)$ the same scalar $a=f(\alpha)$ for all these tuples. The orthogonal sum of these differences is nilpotent with the common exponent $D$ of that step. Hence every central element of the summand has the form $ae+u$ with $u$ nilpotent. The scalar $a$ is unique: a nonzero scalar multiple of $e$ is invertible in this nonzero summand and cannot be nilpotent. As the center is commutative, sums of commuting nilpotents and their products with any central element are nilpotent. Thus its nilpotents form an ideal, the scalar map is a surjective ring homomorphism onto $k$, and every element with nonzero scalar is invertible by the finite geometric series. The center is local over the original field $k$, without extending scalars.

*Induction side.* The same computation with $n$ replaced by $d+1$ shows that $e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}=e_\alpha^{(d)}P_{d+1,i}$ is an idempotent of $kS_{d+1}$ commuting with $kS_d$, that $\sum_{i,\alpha}e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}=1$ with pairwise orthogonal summands, and that $kS_{d+1}=\bigoplus_{i,\alpha}kS_{d+1}e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}$; hence for any finite-dimensional $M$, $$kS_{d+1}\otimes_{kS_d}M=\bigoplus_{i,\alpha}kS_{d+1}e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}\otimes_{kS_d}e_\alpha M=\bigoplus_iF_iM,$$ the middle step using $M=\bigoplus_\alpha e_\alpha M$ and the centrality of $e_\alpha$ in $kS_d$. This is $\operatorname{Ind}M=\bigoplus_iF_iM$.

*Primitivity and exhaustiveness.* A central idempotent $b$ in $e kS_n$ has scalar $0$ or $1$ by step 5.2. In the first case $b$ is nilpotent and idempotent, so $b=0$; in the second case $e-b$ is nilpotent and idempotent, so $b=e$. Thus each nonzero $e_\alpha$ is primitive central. Their orthogonal sum is $1$ by step 4.1. Any primitive central idempotent $b$ of $kS_n$ decomposes as $\sum_\alpha be_\alpha$ into orthogonal central idempotents; primitivity leaves exactly one nonzero term, and the primitivity of that $e_\alpha$ forces $b=e_\alpha$. By [F6] these are precisely the block idempotents. At rank zero $kS_0=k$ and $e(\varnothing)=1$ gives the unique block; restriction from rank zero is taken to be the zero functor, while induction to rank one has only residue $0$. This convention does not invoke a group $S_{-1}$.

*Exactness and duality.* Each $E_i$ is a direct sum of the functors $M\mapsto e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}M$; a map $f:M\to N$ of $kS_n$-modules commutes with the action of the element $e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}$, so it restricts to a map $e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}M\to e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}N$, and each such functor is exact as a direct summand of the identity, hence additive and finite-dimensionality preserving. Each $F_i$ is a direct sum of the functors $M\mapsto kS_{d+1}e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}\otimes_{kS_d}e_\alpha M$, which are direct summands of induction $M\mapsto kS_{d+1}\otimes_{kS_d}M$; by [F5] $kS_{d+1}$ is free as a right $kS_d$-module, so induction, and with it each $F_i$, is exact, additive and finite-dimensionality preserving. For duality observe that $e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}$ is fixed by the antipode by step 1.2, and that the standard nondegenerate pairing $M\times M^*\to k$ satisfies $(xm,f)=(m,x^*f)$; hence for finite-dimensional $M$ the transpose of the projection on $M$ is the projection on $M^*$ and $(e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}M)^*\cong e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}M^*$, giving $E_i(M)^*\cong E_i(M^*)$. All these restriction-duality identifications are $k$-linear and natural.

*Induction duality by a perfect coset pairing.* Put $G=S_{d+1}$, $H=S_d$, and let $\pi_H:kG\to kH$ retain the coefficients of the elements of $H$. For a finite-dimensional left $kH$-module $M$, with contragredient action $(a f)(m)=f(a^{-1}m)$, define $\langle g\otimes m,h\otimes f\rangle=f(\pi_H(h^{-1}g)m)$ between $\operatorname{Ind}M$ and $\operatorname{Ind}M^*$. For $a\in H$, the $kH$-bimodule property of $\pi_H$ gives $\pi_H(h^{-1}ga)=\pi_H(h^{-1}g)a$ and $\pi_H((ha)^{-1}g)=a^{-1}\pi_H(h^{-1}g)$; these identities prove balancing in the first and second tensor factors, respectively. Simultaneous left multiplication of $g,h$ by any element of $G$ leaves $h^{-1}g$ unchanged, proving $G$-invariance. On a finite left-coset transversal $T$ one has $\pi_H(s^{-1}r)=\delta_{s,r}1$ for $r,s\in T$. Thus the pairing is the direct sum of the perfect evaluations $M\times M^*\to k$ and is perfect by [F5]. For $e=e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}$, right multiplication $R_e(g\otimes m)=ge\otimes m$ is a well-defined $G$-linear idempotent because $e$ commutes with $kH$. Let $\tau:kG\to k$ be the coefficient of $1$; directly on group elements, $\tau(xy)=\tau(yx)$. For every $b\in H$, the coefficient of $b$ in $ze$ equals $\tau(b^{-1}ze)=\tau(eb^{-1}z)=\tau(b^{-1}ez)$, since $e$ commutes with $b$. Therefore $\pi_H(ze)=\pi_H(ez)$ for all $z\in kG$. Writing $e^*$ for its antipode image, step 1.2 gives $e^*=e$, so expansion in the group basis yields $\langle R_e(g\otimes m),h\otimes f\rangle=f(\pi_H(h^{-1}ge)m)=f(\pi_H(eh^{-1}g)m)=\langle g\otimes m,R_e(h\otimes f)\rangle$. The two images of $R_e$ pair perfectly: a vector in either image annihilating the other annihilates the entire opposite space, since the opposite kernel is orthogonal to that image, and hence vanishes by perfectness. By tensor balancing, $ge\otimes m=ge\otimes e_\alpha m$, so these images are precisely $kG e\otimes_{kH}e_\alpha M$ and $kG e\otimes_{kH}e_\alpha M^*$. Distinct $e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}$ images are orthogonal by self-adjointness and projector orthogonality. Summing the perfect image pairings over $\alpha\in\mathcal C_d$ proves the natural $G$-isomorphism $F_i(M^*)\cong F_i(M)^*$; invariance supplies the contragredient action, and evaluation shows naturality in $M$. The construction uses finite transversals and holds over every characteristic, including $2$.

*Partition content agrees with the block content.* Let $\lambda\vdash n$ and let $\alpha$ be the multiset of its node contents reduced modulo $p$. Over $\mathbb C$, [F2] makes every elementary symmetric $C_s$ act on $S^\lambda$ by the integer $c_s(\lambda)$. In the integral basis of [F8] the matrix of $C_s-c_s(\lambda)$ has integer entries and vanishes after tensoring with $\mathbb C$, so it vanishes integrally and after specialization to $k$. Thus the CRT polynomial $Q_\alpha(C_1,\ldots,C_n)$ of step 4.1 acts as $1$ on $S^\lambda_k$, while the other content projections act as zero. The same is true on its nonzero subquotients. Hence any simple module obtained from this Specht module belongs to the block $e_\alpha$, establishing the stated content dictionary without a splitting-field descent or a reduced interpolation denominator.
